title: A Secret Theater Underground: Brooklyn Subway Gets a Sparkly Surprise
summary: Have you ever been on a subway and thought, "This is boring"? Well, at the Church Avenue station in Brooklyn, that's not a problem anymore. Artist Christopher Myers created four giant, sparkly mosaics that turn the station into a secret theater. More than 10,000 people see them every day! Myers spent months digging into Flatbush's past. He found out that the neighborhood used to be full of vaudeville shows—that's like a variety show with comedy, music, and dancing from a long time ago. He also learned about the amazing Afro-Caribbean carnival traditions, like the stilt walkers in the West Indian Day Parade. The mosaics show six figures from that world. The star is Moms Mobley, a famous comedian from the 1960s. She's on stage with a red curtain and a giant hand, ready to make you laugh. Myers says the subway is the most democratic space he's ever shown art in. "I've come here and talked with young kids, and they're curious about the figures," he said. The MTA, which runs the subways, has a program that puts art in stations. They got 306 ideas for this spot, but Myers's research and joyful celebration of community won. Next time you're on the train, look around—you might find a hidden masterpiece!
why_it_matters: Art in everyday places like subways can surprise you and teach you about your community’s history, turning a boring commute into a moment of discovery.

background_read: The Church Avenue station has been a stop on the B and Q subway lines in Brooklyn for over 100 years, serving the Flatbush neighborhood.
Long ago, Flatbush was famous for vaudeville theaters—variety shows with comedians, singers, and dancers—that brought people together from all over.
Every year, Brooklyn hosts the West Indian Day Parade, a huge, colorful celebration of Afro-Caribbean culture filled with music, costumes, and stilt walkers that Myers used as inspiration.

The MTA (the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which runs NYC’s buses and subways) has an arts program that has been adding paintings, mosaics, and sculptures to stations since 1985 to make them more welcoming.
Article_Structure: WHO: Artist Christopher Myers, who researched Flatbush’s history and the MTA’s art program.
WHAT: Created four large sparkly mosaics turning the subway into a secret theater, showing figures from vaudeville and Caribbean carnival traditions.
WHERE: Church Avenue subway station in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York.
WHY: To celebrate the hidden history of Flatbush’s vaudeville past and Afro-Caribbean culture, and to bring joyful, free art to thousands of daily riders.

perspectives.description: They love that the mosaics shine a light on forgotten stories like the vaudeville theaters and the stilt walkers of the West Indian Day Parade, making the station a free museum that honors the neighborhood’s roots.
Some might rush past without noticing, but on a quiet day the bright colors and giant figures can make them stop and smile, turning an ordinary train ride into something special.
They believe public art makes stations safer and more interesting, and they picked this project from 306 ideas because it connected so deeply with Flatbush’s unique culture.
